result:
The other day, I found an old shoebox tucked under my bed, its edges frayed with time. Inside were yellowed ticket stubs from a concert I’d forgotten about, a half-melted chocolate bar from a road trip in 2012, and a single, crumpled origami crane my little sister had made me when I was sick. I sat there for a while, running my fingers over the brittle paper, wondering how something so small could hold so much weight—memories, emotions, the quiet proof that I’d once been a kid who believed in magic, in the idea that life was a string of bright, unbroken moments.

It made me think about how we collect things—physical and otherwise. The photos on our phones, the playlists we never skip, the way certain smells (rain on pavement, my grandmother’s perfume) can transport us back to a time we’ve tried to outrun. There’s a comfort in nostalgia, but also a sadness, because it reminds us that time doesn’t just move forward—it erases. The future is always a mystery, but the past is a ghost we carry with us, whispering in the static of our thoughts.

I don’t know why I’m writing this. Maybe because today felt heavy, and words are a way to lighten the load, even if just for a moment. Maybe because I wanted to remember that the small things—the forgotten shoebox, the origami crane—are the ones that stitch us together. Or maybe I just needed to hear myself think out loud.

The crane was still intact, despite the years. I unfolded it carefully, as if it might break, and for a second, I swore I heard the rustle of paper wings. Then I laughed at myself and tucked it back into the box, where it belongs. Some things aren’t meant to be fixed. They’re just meant to be kept.
